newsitem.title: CANADA: PLUGGED IN: Net servants who do windows.
newsitem.headline: PLUGGED IN: Net servants who do windows.

text.p: These days it's not so hard to get good help.
Perhaps one still has trouble lining up people who will do windows and clean out the coffee grinds, but on the Net the personnel crisis is less acute.
In fact, special agents are lining up at your door every digital second to do all the dirty work for you out on the big World Wide Web.

And best of all they will work for a song. Yep, these agents will search out all the information you need (and then some), package it up pretty and deliver it to your door anytime day or night. All you have to do is put up with the odd banner ad and the like.

Of course, in official Internet lingo this is called "Push" technology. It was supposed to be the Next Really, Really Big Thing and -- guess what? -- it's here! Well the tip of this new digital iceberg at least.
There are at least a dozen major companies already pushing the Push ideology, paced by Push grandaddy, PointCast, which can deliver a news and entertainment package to your cyber door by the second.

Netscape Communications Corp. announced last week that the latest release of its Navigator software will incorporate technology from Push pioneer Marimba Inc. to allow access to "channels" of information to surfers. Navigator will incorporate Marimba's tuner right into its browser so users can keep a number of channels or programs ready for viewing at all times.
This opens another front in the so-called browser war between Netscape and Microsoft Corp. and of course we all know that once these two start bickering then the technology should be taken seriously.

Microsoft announced in March its own standard for Push called "Channel Definition Format," and some 30 companies have announced support for the standard, including PointCast. Microsoft, not to be left behind in the Push field, also said the latest version of its browser, Internet Explorer 4.0, will embrace the standard to "enable any Web sit to be a Web broadcaster."

Another sign of maturity in the new technology is the belief that while all this is going on many Web pundits have begun to feel Push is passe -- even before many have yet to feel even the smallest of shoves from a Push vendor. Wired Magazine declared it "tired" in its May edition, just an issue or two after writing a breathless report at the front of the magazine on the coming Push phenomenon.
"I think push has been overhyped" Joe Firmage, chief executive officer of USWeb said recently.
But if you really look at the current Push offerings in the field, you can see they do show some early promise.
Marimba's Castanet technology pushes some interesting "channels," including the Sesame Street KidSite, MapQuest, Commentary and Crossword -- to name a few.

The channels available now seem fun on the surface, not unlike the interactivity you would get from a CD-ROM. But the advantage is that the offerings are constantly updated as the tuner is doing the work for you and constantly updating your programs.

Besides entertainment style channels there are also more practical services. The MapQest channel, for example, offers an amazing ability to view the world in an Atlas format as well as allowing you to zoom into cities and find main thoroughfares or even the smallest of side streets.

Once you download the free tuner from Marimba (www.marimba.com) the channels can be conveniently accessed from the "start" button on your Windows 95 program. This means any time you want to turn on a channel it is right there. And unlike television, the program is not already in progress, as your hired help on the Net is delivering, without complaints, the latest updates seamlessly to your computer.
